@@60420253 <p> U.S. carbon dioxide emissions rose an estimated 3.4 per cent in 2018 , according to new research -- a jarring increase that comes as scientists say the world needs to be aggressively cutting its emissions to avoid the most devastating effects of climate change . <p> The findings , published Tuesday by the independent economic research firm Rhodium Group , mean that the United States now has a diminishing chance of meeting its pledge under the 2015 Paris climate agreement to dramatically reduce its emissions by 2025 . <p> The findings also underscore how the world 's second-largest emitter , once a global leader in pushing for climate action , has all but abandoned efforts to mitigate the effects of a warming world . U.S. President Donald Trump has said he plans to officially withdraw the nation from the Paris climate agreement in 2020 and in the meantime has rolled back Obama-era regulations aimed at reducing the country 's carbon emissions . <p> " We have lost momentum . There 's no question , " Rob Jackson , a Stanford University professor who studies emissions trends , said of both U.S. and global efforts to steer the world @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ think you would have seen the same increase <p> The sharp emissions rise was fueled primarily by a booming economy , researchers found . But the increase , which could prove to be the second-largest in the past 20 years , probably would not have been as stark without Trump administration rollbacks , said Trevor Houser , a partner at Rhodium . <p> " I do n't think you would have seen the same increase , " Houser said , referring to the electric power sector in particular . <p> Emissions from electric power generation rose 1.9 per cent in 2018 , the analysis found , driven chiefly by more demand for electricity , which was largely satisfied by more burning of natural gas . This fuel emits less greenhouse gas than coal when burned but is still a major contributor overall . <p> At the same time , emissions from the transportation sector rose 1 per cent thanks to more airline travel and greater on-road shipping . Industrial emissions from factories and other major facilities also rose significantly in 2018 , the analysis found . <p> The figures , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ other sources , remain an estimate because some data from last year is not finalized . But the trend line is consistent with a recent estimate from a group of academics associated with the Global Carbon Project , which found U.S. emissions likely to rise 2.5 per cent in 2018 . <p> Rising emissions are not just a U.S. problem . Global emissions also reached a record high in 2018 , and the increase in the United States goes hand in hand with rising emissions in other countries , such as China and India , said Michael Mehling , deputy director of the Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology . <p> " It 's not an isolated phenomenon , " Mehling said , adding that the trend makes it difficult to solely blame the Trump administration 's deregulatory push and its dismissal of climate action for the change . " Such political developments , including the rollback of domestic climate policies in the U.S. , tend to have a considerable lead time before you can actually see their reflection in physical emission trends @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ participants at a summit on climate change involving mayors from around the globe Tuesday , Dec. 5 , 2017 , in Chicago.Charles Rex Arbogast/AP file photo <p> The latest growth makes it increasingly unlikely that the United States will achieve a pledge made by the Obama administration in the run-up to the Paris climate agreement , that the country would reduce its greenhouse gas emissions by 26 to 28 per cent below 2005 levels by the year 2025 . <p> A large part of President Barack Obama 's plan for meeting that goal turned on key climate policies , including new regulations for vehicle fuel efficiency and power plants . These policies alone were not enough -- the United States has never been on target to fulfill its Paris promises . But the Trump administration has moved to reverse or weaken them . <p> U.S. emissions have declined somewhat since 2005 because of technological changes , such as the dwindling of coal-fired power generation in the face of surging natural gas and the growth of renewable energy . @@60420994 <h> Human-induced climate change strongly linked to BC wildfires <p> Human influences played a major role in BC 's 2017 wildfire season and significantly increased the risk of wildfires , says a study by research scientists from the Pacific Climate Impacts Consortium at the University of Victoria and Environment and Climate Change Canada . <p> The research , published in the open-access journal Earth 's Future , used climate simulations to compare two scenarios -- one included realistic human influence on the climate , while the other factored minimal human influence . Researchers found that the extreme high temperatures were made 20 times more likely by human-induced climate change . They also found the area burned seven to 11 times larger than would have been expected without human influence on the climate . Extreme temperatures combined with dry conditions increase the likelihood of wildfire ignition and its spread . <p> 1.2 million hectares burned during the 2017 BC wildfire season -- a record that was surpassed in 2018 . <p> UVic is a leader in research on climate modelling , mitigation and adaptation , the development of sustainable energy systems , and the human dimensions of climate change . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to foster clean growth , sustainable solutions and low-carbon economic development to address the challenges posed by climate change . <h> Media contacts <p> Media Relations and Public Affairs provides a range of services for journalists , including finding UVic experts for stories , arranging interviews and photo/filming opportunities about UVic research and programs , and providing photos and videos and other materials for use in news coverage . 
@@60421117 <h> Researchers suggest global warming increased area burned up to 11 times <p> At the time , 2017 was the worst wildfire season on record in B.C. , until a new record was set the following summer . ( Darryl Dyck/Canadian Press ) <p> The record-breaking B.C. wildfires of 2017 may have burned as much as 11 times more land than they would have without the influence of human-caused climate change , according to new research . <p> The study , from scientists at the Pacific Climate Impacts Consortium at the University of Victoria and Environment and Climate Change Canada , suggests that climate change was the driving factor for the unusually hot conditions that led to the fires . The probability of abnormally high temperatures being caused by global warming was estimated at more than 95 per cent . <p> " We have demonstrated that human-induced climate change has significantly increased the likelihood of extreme high temperatures , of extreme wildfire risk of large areas burned , similar to what we saw in the 2017 wildfire season in B.C. , " Kirchmeier-Young told CBC . <p> More than 1.2 million hectares of B.C. burned in 2017 , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . By almost every metric , it was the worst season on record -- that is , until the summer of 2018 , when more than 1.35 million hectares went up in flames . <p> Though researchers have long said that climate change is responsible for a trend toward longer and more destructive wildfire seasons , it 's been more difficult to directly connect a single disastrous summer to global warming . <p> To make that link , the researchers used a technique called event attribution analysis.It 's a method that compares how likely a certain natural disaster might be on a planet affected by human-caused climate change than it would be in a more untouched world . <p> Because most global warming has been seen since the 1970s , Kirchmeier-Young and her colleagues compared conditions from 1961-1970 to those from today and took into account the human activities that drive climate change , including greenhouse gas emissions and changes in land use . <h> Increased wildfire activity likely in the future <p> They found that the extreme fire risks of 2017 were made two to four times more likely @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ increased by a factor of seven to 11 times . <p> That does n't bode well for the future . <p> " If we see the temperature trends continue , then increased temperatures in the future result in increased wildfire , " Kirchmeier-Young said . <p> The researchers did not find evidence of how anthropogenic factors influenced rainfall -- on top of being unusually hot , the summer of 2017 was also abnormally dry . <p> They also point out that there are still uncertainties about how non-climatic factors contributed to the record-breaking fires . Poor forest management practices including a lack of controlled burning , for example , have also been blamed for some of the damage caused by wildfires in recent years . <h> About the Author <p> Bethany Lindsay <p> Journalist <p> Bethany Lindsay has more than a decade of experience in B.C. journalism , with a focus on the courts , health and social justice issues . The dictionary defines capitalism as " an economic system characterized by private or corporate ownership of capital goods , by investments that are determined by private decision , and by prices , production , and the distribution of goods that are determined mainly by competition in a free market . " <p> We can look to the U.S. to see the results of lowering taxes , deregulating industries , and the increasing divide between haves and have-nots : health care and social security for those outside the " elite " class are taking a beating . We do n't want this to happen in Canada . <p> Health care needs the creativity , innovation , risk tolerance , and nimbleness of private companies , but these criteria need to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with public oversight . Public and private delivery of health services can work , but require strong public leadership , a new philosophy , and corporations that accept the balance of a healthy , productive workforce , a good place to live , and are invested in the long game ( rather than quick profits at any cost ) . <p> We welcome the recently publicized federal airline passenger bill of rights , with its clear standards and penalties . We need a similar " patient bill of rights " in Nova Scotia , to establish clear standards , outcome measurements and reporting requirements to hold providers accountable . We can lead this . <p> Health care needs the creativity , innovation , risk tolerance , and nimbleness of private companies , but these criteria need to operate within a strong set of rules , regulations and with public oversight . <p> My last suggestion is to break the current administrative logjam . China continues to view Taiwan as a renegade province . <p> The Taiwanese-Canadian community , concentrated in Metro Vancouver and Greater Toronto , has a population of close to 200,000 . <p> Charlie Wu , managing director of the Asian-Canadian Special Events Association and the organizer of the annual TaiwanFest in Vancouver and Toronto , said Taiwanese Canadians and businesses have always been acutely aware of the fine line they walk . <p> While Wu faces a different version of that balancing act -- Air Canada is a key TaiwanFest sponsor -- he hopes the controversy will focus more public attention on the issue . <p> " Perhaps this exercise of working with Air Canada and Taiwan-Fest , allowing people to learn about the festival and Taiwan , may provide businesses with some perspectives to think about how @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Do I really have to stand on one side , or is there a way I can be more creative , so as not to be seen as bowing to pressure ? " <p> Canada 's 2016 merchandise trade with Taiwan reached $1.54 billion in exports and $5.08 billion in imports ; its trade with China during the same period was $20.1 billion in exports and $64.4 billion in imports . <p> Simon said Taiwan is one of several concerns Canadian companies have with doing business in China . <p> He noted that , because foreign companies have no property rights in China , they are vulnerable to sudden changes in regulations . <p> He cited the example of Starbucks ( Nasdaq:SBUX ) opening a caf ? in Beijing 's Forbidden City in 2000 , then suddenly being forced to close in 2007 due to backlash from Chinese domestic media . <p> While Canadian businesses wait for legal protection from Ottawa , Simon said companies such as Tim Hortons ( Nasdaq:THI ) , which announced in July it plans to open 1,500 stores in China in a joint venture , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ potential risk . <p> Lerhe 's report notes that governments in New Zealand , Australia , Germany , Japan and the United States joined Canada in supporting Taiwanese inclusion in the World Health Assembly and World Health Organization , which signifies that some western countries have shown a willingness to draw the line somewhere with Beijing . " Canada should work with its allies to develop a prioritized action list of other international organizations that Taiwan should be a member of , such as the International Civil Aviation Organization , Interpol and the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change , " Lerhe wrote . <p> " Any one of these actions will undoubtedly produce the usual hyperbolic outrage from China . But ... almost all of the recommendations are based on actions some other western-oriented nation has already taken . " <p> For Wu , part of the solution is to support Canadian businesses while understanding the headwinds they face occasionally from Beijing . <p> " If you see Air Canada as the national carrier , it 's the Canadian airline , " said Wu , whose TaiwanFest has thrived @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in Vancouver and Toronto . <p> " If , today , Canadian businesses get treated badly in the world , will we stand behind them ? Obviously , we will . I think we need to see that they have gotten some pressure , and maybe they need to find a way to balance it . We want to offer them a different perspective . " <p> Simon agreed . He added that an example of how Canadian government and businesses should act is found in Canada 's own history . <p> " You know , Air Canada never went along with the U.S. embargo against Cuba ; they found ways around that . For quite a long time , many Canadian firms did n't go along with that .... We have to unite around our right to say no to foreign governments . If we can say no to the United States , we can say no to China as well . "

@@60425532 <h> Human-induced climate change fanning wildfires , study reports <p> The Philpot Road wildfire burns just outside of Kelowna in August 2017 . <p> Photograph By Jonathan Hayward , The Canadian Press <p> Humans played a substantial role in making B.C. wildfires in 2017 bigger and more likely , says a new study by UVic and the federal government . <p> Published in Earth 's Future , the study , by the Pacific Climate Impact Consortium at the University of Victoria and Environment and Climate Change Canada , says 2017 's " anomalously " hot summer temperatures were made 20 times more likely by human-induced climate change . <p> Researchers also found that the area burned by wildfires was seven to 11 times larger than would have been expected without human-induced climate change . Extreme warm temperatures combined with dry conditions increase the likelihood that fires will start and spread . <p> Francis Zwiers , director of the Pacific Climate Impacts Consortium and one of the study 's authors , said the research was conducted using computer models and data collected over many decades . <p> The study used present conditions , including levels of greenhouse gases , to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from 1961 through 1970 , when the influence of human emissions was substantially lower and much of the observed global warming had not yet occurred . <p> Researchers took the measure of 2017 's wildfire risk from an index developed by Natural Resources Canada and calculated how likely it would be for that risk level to occur under both scenarios . <p> The study looked at the dry , hot summer conditions in 2017 as a contributor to the risk of wildfires . High temperatures , such as those seen that summer , make wildfires more likely and bigger . <p> " Human influence on the climate system has substantially increased the likelihood of very hot summers , " Zwiers said . " These very hot conditions contribute to wildfire risk . <p> " And we can now expect when there is a fire as a consequence of human influence that fire will be bigger . " <p> Neither forestry practices nor impacts such as the mountain pine beetle were taken into account , the paper acknowledges . But researchers say the findings are consistent with those of many other @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> The 2017 fires forced about 65,000 people from their homes and destroyed 509 structures , including 229 homes . The province spent more than $522 million fighting the blazes . In all , 1.2 million hectares burned , setting a new record . The previous record , 870,000 hectares burned , was set in 1958 . <p> Last year was even worse , with 1.35 million hectares burned . <p> Zwiers said making predictions about consequences is always difficult . The overall climate is warming up , but local weather events -- such as El Ni ? o , for example -- can inject all kinds of variables . <p> " Inter-annual variability still plays a huge role , but in the background , we have this warming effect that wo n't go away , " he said . " That warming effect is driving up the likelihood of these kinds of extreme events . "

@@60426118 <p> Dr. Dianne Saxe , Ontario 's Environmental Commissioner , is pointing at a graph projected on a wall at Calvin Presbyterian Church . <p> The lines on the left side of the graph -- the early years of the 20th century -- are almost uniformly below the centreline . <p> The latter half of the chart is almost exactly the opposite . Virtually all are above the centreline . <p> The centreline is the average temperature -- what used to be called normal . <p> " We do n't live there anymore , " Saxe told about 75 people at the presentation . <p> " Normal is gone . It 's not coming back . " <p> Climate change is real , no matter what some people might say , Saxe stresses . " <p> And the concentration is increasing -- and at a faster pace -- every year . <p> The problem is even worse in Ontario , which is warming at a faster pace than the global average . @@60429065 <h> It 's Time to Talk About Ecological Grief <p> This story was originally published by Undark and appears here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration . <p> When I called Courtney Howard , one of the authors of the recent Lancet Countdown 2018 Report on health and climate change , she was Christmas shopping during a pit stop in London on her way to the 24th United Nations Climate Change Conference in Katowice , Poland . <p> As she picked out ballet shoes for one of her young daughters , we discussed her work on the mental health impacts of climate change . She recounted to me the moment in her own life when climate change 's bottom line really sunk in . She was at home with her daughter doing some mental math : Yellowknife , the capital of Canada 's Northwest Territories , where she lives , was already 2.5 degrees Celsius warmer than it was in the 1940s , and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change ( IPCC ) had recently reported that average global temperatures were on pace to warm another half degree or more by 2052 . The warming would be irreversible @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ lifetime of her children . She wound up on the floor , wrapped around her daughter in the fetal position . <p> The impact of climate change on our physical world has by now been made clear and manifest to anyone paying attention : Rising sea levels and increasing temperatures have begotten wildfires , drought , tsunamis and heat waves , which have wrought unprecedented devastation . The impact of climate change on our internal worlds , though , has gone relatively unstudied . But a growing body of evidence demonstrates that climate change and its effects are linked to elevated rates of depression , anxiety , suicidal ideation , post-traumatic stress , and a host of negative emotions including anger , hopelessness , despair , and a feeling of loss . Researchers have dubbed these feelings " ecological grief . " <p> In a briefing for Canadian policymakers released in conjunction with the Lancet Countdown , Howard and her colleagues honed in on ecological grief , eco-anxiety , and something called solastalgia -- a form of homesickness one experiences while still at home . Grief and mourning are natural @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ through . Research shows that the sixth mass extinction is underway , and the World Health Organization named climate change the single greatest threat to global health this century . <p> Ecological grief is the grief that 's felt in response to experienced or anticipated ecological loss . It may arise due to acute environmental disasters . For example , one in six survivors of Hurricane Katrina met the criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder , and crop-damaging heat waves have been shown to lead to increased suicide rates in India . But grief can also stem from stress and anxiety associated with slow , creeping changes in one 's environment -- feelings that many of us are experiencing as the winters become uncannily warmer and extreme weather events become more frequent . <p> Communities whose livelihoods and ways of living are inextricable from their natural environments , though , are on the frontlines of the crisis . In the Inuit communities of Nunatsiavut , located in the north of Canada 's most easterly province , Newfoundland and Labrador , temperatures are warming twice as fast as in the rest of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , shorter winters , and unpredictable weather . Like other public health challenges , the burden of climate change 's mental health impacts falls primarily on groups that are already vulnerable . The losses these communities suffer extend to every corner of their lives , and they 're unending , says Ashlee Cunsolo , the director of the Labrador Institute of Memorial University and another contributor to the recent Lancet report . The land -- or ice -- is literally shifting beneath their feet and before their eyes . The attendant grief these communities experience is similarly amorphous and ubiquitous . <p> The changing landscape brings food insecurity , post-traumatic stress disorder , population displacement , and trauma . There are no roads in or out of Nunatsiavut 's Rigolet , the southernmost Inuit community in Canada . The town is accessible by ice road , by plane , or -- during the summer months -- by ferry . In recent years , the ice has started to form a month later and melt a month earlier , says Derrick Pottle , a hunter and commercial trapper . And when @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ go . Without the ice road , " you 're trapped -- even if you wanted to get out you could n't . " For Pottle and the rest of the community , the sea and the land are " our highways , how we move around , how we get out to harvest , and how we connect to the land . " <p> Historically , the Inuit have depended on their natural environment for survival . To lose it is to lose not only the ability to visit friends and family , but also the ability to provide for one 's family by hunting , fishing , and foraging . The land is also foundational to a sense of well-being and belonging , contributing to people 's ability to live their cultural lives in a healthy way . To watch helplessly as the landscapes , ecosystems , species , and places that carried collective meaning become unrecognizable before your eyes is painful . Community members in Rigolet report feelings of fear , anxiety , sadness , anger , frustration , and hopelessness . They worry about what the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ about what future environmental changes will mean for their way of life . These intense negative emotions can lead to additional mental health burdens , such as increases in drug and alcohol use , domestic violence , and suicide . <p> Ecological loss can also lead to a crisis of culture and identity . In the 2014 documentary about climate change in Rigolet , " Lament for the Land , " an existential question is posed : " Inuit are people of the sea ice . If there is no more sea ice , how can we be people of the sea ice ? " This kind of mourning is what Cunsolo calls disenfranchised grief : a grief that is n't publicly or openly acknowledged . When we grieve the loss of a person , we come together with other people and perform rituals to work through these elements of grief . But when it 's the loss of place , or the degradation of a body of water , or when a species collapses , there are simply no rituals in place for processing the loss . <p> The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ collective mourning , as large expanses of the planet become uninhabitable and more of us begin to experience the loss of our environments as we knew them . As Cunsolo and Howard continue to research ecological grief , they 've both found that after they share their findings in public , there 's often a deluge of people who come to them to share their experiences of stress , anxiety , depression , and hopelessness in the face of our changing climate . Research like theirs quantifies the psychological toll of climate change , giving policy makers and health professionals the evidence they need to account for it as part of the human cost of global warming . Ecological grief is not new , but there 's power in being able to name it , and there 's relief in being able to share it . <p> As climate change marches forward , the tangible mental health effects of ecological grief will mount : loss of work hours , increased costs and burdens on health systems , and untimely death . But grief can either paralyze you or galvanize you @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ table in climate discussions , but the language of ecological grief adds weight to the science , statistics , policies , and politics of climate change . It makes it clear what is at stake -- and what 's at stake are our lives as we know them . <p> By beginning to pay attention to these intangible losses , we can expand the narrative of climate change and find ways to support one another , encourage action , and create healthy communities . At the end of our call , Howard , nearly done with her shopping , gave me a prescription to do just that : Get outside for some fresh air , spend time with friends and family , and spend 20 minutes a day taking action against climate change . <h> Comments <p> If this grief does n't move us to action , it 's hard to know what will . Problem is , climate change is a wicked problem in that its effects are often visited on the most vulnerable , and therefore , the least powerful , first . We need vast amounts of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cooperatives , need to act while we have the capacity to make a difference . And I 'm not talking about talking to our leaders .... voting them out would make more sense , if they cater to old white folks who still global warming is a hoax . But the remediation I favour is boycotting tropical beaches and using some of that disposable income to retrofit , solarize , invest in , and invent restorative activities . <p> We are n't helpless quite yet ..... but without citizen action , that day is coming for city dwellers , just as it is here now for the people of the Arctic . Change is hard , but it can also be exhilarating . <p> That prescription is a bit Procrustean . These days , my nature access looks like a mine site , so I get my exercise and such other ways . @@60429708 <p> In 2008 , B.C. implemented North America 's first carbon tax , which survived the global crash while the BC Liberals were reelected . France could take a lesson why . Photo by eclecctica , Creative Commons licensed . <p> If we 're ever going to get to a carbon neutral or carbon negative economy , placing a price on carbon is going to be a necessary part of that effort . <p> But just because strong action is needed that can be implemented both rapidly and at large scales , it does n't follow that the consequences of these actions on people either can or should be ignored . <p> That 's particularly true when it comes to the working poor and middle class . <p> As we 've seen in France and other countries over the past weeks , taxes targeting fossil fuels wo n't receive the kind of public support they 're going to need if they 're implemented without sufficient regard for the people paying them . <p> Fortunately , there is a proven solution that facilitates the carbon dioxide emission reductions that carbon taxes are intended to achieve while also taking into account @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the carbon tax revenue neutral , taking special care to use the money it generates to prioritize tax reductions for the poor , middle class and rural residents affected most . <p> This is precisely what British Columbia did when it implemented North America 's first carbon tax in 2008 . That this tax survived the financial crisis that reached its zenith just two months after its implementation is a testament to the fact that even during the worst of times a skeptical and insecure public can still be persuaded to support a policy if it truly reconciles environmental protection with equity and fairness . <p> Gradual and revenue neutral <p> As in the French countryside , residents of rural B.C. often have no choice but to drive long distances on a regular basis . Unlike their fellow citizens in cities like Vancouver and Victoria , public transportation opportunities frequently do n't exist or are insufficient to completely replace the automobile . <p> When the carbon tax was first imposed in July 2008 , it started small . It began at $10 per tonne with incremental annual increases of $5 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ That meant that by July 2012 the cost of gasoline would rise by 6.67 cents per litre . For American readers , that amounts to approximately 27 cents per gallon . To put that in perspective , the gas tax the French government had been planning to impose next month amounted to roughly 25 cents per gallon . <p> But unlike B.C. , France was moving to implement its tax in one fell swoop , and it had no plans to either offset the gasoline tax increase with middle and low-income tax cuts or to use the revenue to provide other significant tangible benefits . As the B.C. experiment with carbon taxes shows , phasing in the tax and making it revenue neutral is crucial to winning public support for any carbon tax that 's going to be significant enough to make a difference . <p> One study into the effectiveness of the B.C. carbon tax described the steps the then Liberal government took to achieve revenue neutrality this way : <p> First , the B.C. government lowered the tax rate on the bottom two personal income tax brackets . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the average provincial tax rate was reduced from 8.74 per cent in 2007 to 8.02 per cent in 2008 . Two lump-sum transfers were also included to protect low-income and rural households . Low-income households receive quarterly rebates , which , for a family of four , equal approximately $300 per year , and beginning in 2011 northern and rural homeowners received a further benefit of up to $200 . Finally , taxes on corporations and small businesses were reduced . Since residents ' tax burden did not increase , the government was able to promote the policy as a " tax shift " rather than a tax increase . <p> President Emmanuel Macron eliminated France 's wealth tax in 2017 in advance of his proposed gas tax increase , not in concert with it , so it proved impossible to claim that ending that tax was part of an effort to implement some sort of revenue-neutral carbon tax " shift . " <p> More importantly , however , by putting the wealth tax repeal first and failing to offer low-income and rural households additional tax breaks to offset the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to let the poor and middle class carry most of the burden when it came to taxes on carbon . Had the BC Liberal government followed a similar approach in 2008 , I do n't know if cars would have been burning in downtown Vancouver , but they almost certainly would have been trounced in the following year 's election . <p> Yellow vests , green blindspots <p> Now , just when we need carbon taxes the most , the ' yellow vest ' movement threatens to render them a political third rail few politicians will want to touch . Sadly , most environmentalists cheered Macron 's gas tax proposal when they should have jeered , costing them valuable credibility with working-class voters that they 're going to need for any successful campaign against climate change . <p> The phrase " carbon tax " too often triggers a kind of Pavlovian response in the environmental community , regardless of the impact they will have on those paying them . If the environmental policies these times demand are ever going to be implemented on a global scale , then we must @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ separate policy silos . People do n't like being treated as a means to an environmental end any more than they appreciate being treated as a means to any other end , nor should they . <p> Yellow Vest protests in Belfort , France in November , part of nationwide revolt triggered by imposition of a gas tax as a wealth tax was rescinded . Photo by Thomas Bresson , Creative Commons licensed via Wikimedia . <p> Carbon taxes , whether they are revenue neutral or not , will , unfortunately , usually face stiff opposition in the beginning . In B.C. , the major opposition party had been in favour of taxing carbon , but it flip-flopped when the opportunity to tag the Liberal Party with the initially unpopular policy presented itself just prior to an election year . <p> That said , the BC Liberal Party ( rather confusingly B.C. 's most conservative major party ) was able to retain control of the B.C. government in 2009 in spite of everything . In a March 2016 article on B.C. With the help of Green Party members elected to the province 's legislative assembly , the NDP took control of the provincial government in May 2017 . B.C. It is scheduled to hit $50 a tonne one year ahead of the federal government 's proposed carbon tax . <p> That just leaves the question of whether a revenue-neutral approach to carbon taxation can actually reduce carbon emissions . After all , if all the money raised through the tax is ultimately returned to taxpayers in one form or another , where 's the incentive to reduce spending on gasoline , the largest source of CO2 in B.C. ? <p> Well , it has worked . A review of the existing research on the tax 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that up to that point all the studies indicated a reduction in greenhouse gas emissions of around nine per cent and that gasoline sales had dropped anywhere between seven per cent and 17 per cent . @@60431291 <p> This article was originally published on The Conversation , an independent and nonprofit source of news , analysis and commentary from academic experts . Disclosure information is available on the original site . <p> This week , U.S. President Donald Trump gave a live address on prime-time television where he repeatedly used the words " violent , " " illegal aliens " and " crisis " to arouse public fear . While Trump 's speech was based largely on fallacies , his fear-mongering shapes the national tone and can generate real-world impacts . <p> Words matter because they wield power . Words shape our thinking about the world and , in turn , the actions we take . The meaning of words has never been more relevant than now -- in the era of " fake news " -- when so-called alternative facts abound . <p> Environmental words can also be misinterpreted or misused . In the most sinister cases , language can be put to work to promote particular agendas and silence others . <p> Remember " beautiful clean coal ? " The Trump administration used the term as the backbone for the continued development of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ systematically removed the words " climate change " from federal websites , a measure aimed at undermining climate action . <p> Power can be expressed through environmental buzzwords . They are used to influence policy direction , funding and produce norms that become entrenched in their meaning around the world . Motivated by this idea , our recent research explores the meaning of three environmental buzzwords -- resilience , sustainability and transformation . Meaning influences the way we understand environmental problems and shapes the solutions we prioritize -- or do n't . <p> The rise of resilience <p> Let 's begin with " resilience . " Over the past decade , resilience has increasingly become a rallying cry in the face of climatic change . Resilience has many meanings , from the time it takes to bounce back from a disturbance to more complex interpretations that consider the capacity to persist , adapt or transform in the face of change . <p> Evidence shows that individuals , even those who share demographic characteristics or professions , interpret resilience in very different ways . These differences matter and can have implications @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ related to flooding , for example , understanding resilience as bouncing back can lead to decisions to focus solely on infrastructure investments , while a more complex interpretation may lead to a decision to relocate a vulnerable subdivision away from a floodplain . <p> The rise of resilience as a buzzword has also led to its prominence in agendas put forward by organizations looking for funding often without a clear intention or accountability . <p> Sustainability for whom ? <p> The concept of " sustainability " has dominated environmental thinking since the publication of the influential essay " A Blueprint for Survival " in 1972 . The notion of sustainability rests upon the idea that we are obligated to future generations and ought to live in a way that preserves natural resources and environments so that our children and grandchildren can enjoy them . <p> The underlying idea is that we have the technological and scientific know-how and power to achieve this goal . And this definition of sustainability centres on humans . Asking " what is sustainability and who is it for ? " may lead to a surprising @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sustainability raises new questions : Must we work toward preserving natural environments for ourselves ? Is it justified to work toward preserving a species that is harmful to itself and others -- like we have been ? <p> Privileging the well-being of other species over our own -- by significantly reducing our use of highly polluting natural resources -- may help to slow climate change , for example . This requires , however , a radical shift in our thinking , displacing the human from the centre of our preoccupations . <p> Clearly our know-how has not prevented the acceleration of the environmental crisis . Rethinking ourselves as beings that are deeply interconnected with our habitats and those we share it with , as post-humanist thinkers do , could lead to redefining the notion of sustainability and what constitutes an appropriate course of action . Significantly , this new vision of sustainability may not always favour the human . <p> The dark side of transformation <p> " Transformation " is increasingly seen as a solution to many of our planet 's profound environmental and social challenges . For example , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for 2030 to describe radical shifts towards more environmentally sustainable and socially just futures . <p> In contrast , transformation has also been used by struggling political parties to rebrand failing platforms ( essentially selling old wine in a new bottle ) . <p> There are risks associated with misappropriating " transformation " . Put to wrong use , it can conceal harmful business-as-usual scenarios , exclude the possibility of resistance , pay scarce attention to inequality , overlook the role of power or shift the burden of response onto vulnerable parties . <p> For example , a recent report commissioned by the United Kingdom for policy-makers presents climate migration as a positive " transformational " strategy that " will be an extremely effective way to build long-term resilience . " Yet , we know that forced migration can be devastating for climate refugees . <p> So , what now ? <p> No one owns the meaning of words . Yet it 's essential to keep in mind that language is never neutral : it conveys and shapes values , attitudes and intent . This subtle power is particularly troubling @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ more often than factual ones . <p> The words we use ( and the meanings we ascribe to them ) become public truths that set the context for environmental policies , funding and interventions . Closer to home , the recent standoff between members of the Wet'suwet'en First Nation and the RCMP is stimulating reflection on the meaning of the term " self-governing . " <p> Achieving genuinely equitable futures will require each of us to read carefully , think critically and guard against the manipulation of environmental words . As governments and institutions across the world struggle to implement environmental policies and make important decisions on climate change , we would do well to reflect critically on the meaning of the words that inform these processes and be transparent about their multiple interpretations and resulting impacts . <p> -- -- <p> This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license . @@60436316 <h> Sudbury Accent : Lots done , lots still to do , top biologist says <p> Aerial view of Ramsey Lake ( foreground ) and Lake Nepahwin in Sudbury , Ont. on Friday June 22 , 2018 . John Gunn says Sudbury has lots of work to do to protect the city 's lakes and rivers . John Lappa/Sudbury Star/Postmedia Network <p> John Gunn is director of the Living with Lakes Centre in Sudbury and Canada Research Chair in Stressed Aquatic Systems . JOHN LAPPA/THE SUDBURY STAR <p> John Gunn is a fisheries biologist who has for the past 25 years studied the effects of acid rain , climate change , and a variety of other environmental factors on coldwater fish communities . As the director of the Living with Lakes Centre in Sudbury and Canada Research Chair in Stressed Aquatic Systems , he is now leading a team of researchers in the study of the effects of multiple stressors on Shield ecosystems . He is also investigating the recovery processes that operate once stressors are removed . Lakes near Sudbury , are particularly important for the recovery studies . Emissions of air pollutants in this area have declined @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ aquatic systems are beginning to recover . Here , he takes time to answer The Star 's 10 questions . <p> Forests are often described as the lungs of the planet , and freshwater as its lifeblood . Sudbury has plenty of both , although the former was missing for quite a while . Can you talk a bit about the relationship between the two and how regreening has benefited our lakes and rivers ? <p> The recovering forest in Sudbury produces some remarkable interactions with lakes . For example as the trees return to the once-barren landscape ( because of cleaner air and trees planted by the many volunteers ) , the bottom temperatures in the lakes actually begin to cool even while air temperatures rise because of climate warming . One reason for the cooling effect is that the growing trees create texture and drag on the surface winds , slowing them down by almost 35 per cent , thus reducing the wind 's power to mix warm surface waters into the depths where the cold-water species like lake trout live . As the new forest grows , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ litter and rotting vegetation forms a giant " tea bag " of organic matter around the lake . When water flows through the debris it leaches out organic matter ( let 's call it forest tea ) into the lake , creating a sunblock substance that shades the bottom waters from the warming effects of the sun 's radiation , as well as blocking the damaging UV rays ( yes , providing a natural sunscreen ) . This " forest tea " we actually call dissolved organic matter also binds and detoxifies dissolved metals such as copper and nickel that have accumulated in the lakes from past smelter pollution inputs ( thus protecting sensitive fish and insects ) . <p> The growing trees on the hillsides also act like thousands of tall drinking straws that lift water back into the atmosphere as gases and thus reduces the flow of liquid water to the lake . This evaporative effect of trees can greatly reduce -- by more than 50 per cent -- the overland flow of water . With less water flowing into the lake , there is less chance of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that causes those nasty algae blooms . <p> As we know people ca n't live on tea alone , but in our Sudbury research we have learned that the " forest tea " is actually quite nutritious , at least much better than nothing . For example , when we catch a fish and analyze the sources of the carbon that makes up its body , surprisingly sometimes 40-60 per cent comes from forest trees rather than beginning as algae or plants growing in the sunlight within the lake . <p> You have spoken about a 100-year plan for Lake Ramsey that I believe was introduced in the 1990s . Why was that important and how well have we hewed to its vision ? <p> When Raymond Moriyama and Ted Teshima -- the famous Canadian architects who designed the snowflake on the rocky knob we call Science North -- were asked to produce a future-looking plan for Ramsey Lake , they did what few had ever done before . They planned for 100 years , a period of time much longer than the term for a city councillor or of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it takes to grow a forest or for ancient groundwater to make its way underground before popping up in the lake ( consider the cold water seeps at Moonlight Beach ) . Their plan , published in 1991 , saw the lake as " the green and natural heart of the city , a public domain where resources of city-wide importance can be gathered in a magnificent setting and made accessible , a place of enjoyment , discovery and recreation for all the people . " <p> Many aspects of their plan have sprouted and grown , like the beautiful boardwalk ( 1993 ) and recently completed Trans-Canada Trail network , or the fabulous new rowing club next to Science North , the second-largest science " discovery centre " in Canada . Others have not . The risky oil tank cars on the railway still pass above the lake almost every day , and many proposed green spaces have now been converted into mega homes and big-box stores , with little regard for soil management practices . We still have the same minimal 10-metre shoreline setback requirements for residential construction @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ silt fences or in-lake booms to protect the shoreline . <p> What would Raymond and Ted say ? Why ask them ? Instead , let 's give that question to our new homegrown architecture students at the McEwan School downtown . I am sure they would use fresh eyes to tackle these old problems . Perhaps they would get rid of the eyesore that the abandoned hospital represents , or finally find a way to celebrate the city with a place that serves food and music down by the water . I bet they would also come up with more green solutions by insisting new construction uses mainly wood ( to maximize carbon sequestration and support northern forest industries ) rather than designing with concrete , a material that generates so much greenhouse gas , both when produced and transported . <p> There seems to be increasing evidence that drugs entering water systems are having an adverse impact on aquatic species -- birth control pills , for instance , causing infertility in minnows . Should we also be concerned about opioids like fentanyl affecting lake health ? <p> I can @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but as far as I am aware , there is n't currently anyone collecting information in Sudbury lakes to assess how pharmaceuticals might be affecting lake systems downstream of our sewage treatment plants . Our main contaminants of concern within the city lakes are road salt ( discussed later ) , PCBs ( a family of man-made organic chemicals with historical commercial and industrial uses ) and mercury . <p> The really surprising thing about contaminants in fish from our industrial region is how relatively low they are and how rarely the Ministry of Environment has ever issued guidelines ( check out your lake at **45;60;TOOLONG ... to ask people to limit monthly consumption of fish from Sudbury lakes . We do have one lake , Nepahwin , with persistent PCB problems in fish ( presumably originating from some old contaminated soil areas ) , but the contaminant we are mainly concerned about is mercury . Oddly enough , most Sudbury fish have less mercury in them than comparable sizes and species of sportfish in remote lakes in the Far North . Mercury mobilized into the atmosphere from human activities @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ( another good reason for shutting down Ontario 's coal plants ) ends up travelling thousands of kilometres through the atmosphere before being deposited into a lake or its tributaries . The arriving mercury gets converted by bacteria into a form called methylmercury that is able to move up through the food chain , eventually reaching the fish we eat . However , what we and other researchers have learned over the decades is that when mercury interacts with selenium in the water , the methylation and uptake of mercury can be greatly reduced . Now can you guess what we have in Sudbury ? That 's right , elevated amounts of selenium in the lakes , especially in lakes near the smelters where the selenium likely originated . Now if you look on the label of your daily vitamin bottle , you will see that selenium ( Se ) is an essential element . At high concentrations , however , it is quite toxic . Fortunately our lakes appear to have hit the sweet spot , with trace amounts in the water effectively blocking much of the mercury uptake @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ need to keep carefully monitoring , even with the massive reductions of atmospheric emissions of sulphur and metals from the smelters ( now down 99 per cent ) , but in the meantime enjoy your fish for supper . I will , as well . <p> The Vale Living with Lakes Centre , located along the shores of Ramsey Lake.File photo <p> How do you see climate change impacting our water bodies right now and in coming years ? What could Sudbury do to mitigate warming and possibly set an example for other communities ? <p> The truly scary reality we face is that the Paris Accord on Climate Change is in deep trouble , as important countries withdraw and others miss their targets , while big oil , coal and other fossil-fuel companies continue to win the climate battle ( as the big tobacco companies did for decades in the lung cancer war ) . The impacts of climate change on our water bodies will likely get much worse before they get better . Rivers and creeks will be particularly vulnerable to flash flooding , according to the new @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , remembering how devastating floods have been before ( such 22 drowning deaths in Junction Creek in past 100 years ) . <p> Impacts on lakes may be more subtle . For example , when I came to Sudbury in 1978 we were at or about the northern limit for warm water fish such as smallmouth bass -- the winters were too cold and too long for the young bass to make it through without feeding . Instead , cold-water species like brook trout thrived in many of our lakes . For example , Joe Lake was then a lake where anglers frequently won the Molson prize for big trout . Now 30 years later bass thrive throughout the region and are even found in the Moose River , a river that flows into the Arctic Ocean . While bass now thrive in many Sudbury lakes , even creating a tournament fishery on Ramsey Lake , the native cold-water trout are disappearing . In fact brook trout are extinct in lakes like Joe . It is now a bass lake . Lake trout , too , have been severely reduced @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ competition for food is fierce . <p> Lake ice cover will become less predictable for winter sports ( even dangerous , particularly in the shoulder seasons when freeze and thaw timing will be different than what we 're used to ) , and in the summer , you will most likely start to observe that the rocks are getting slippery when you are going swimming . Increasing effects of urban development ( septic tanks , fertilizer ) will be exacerbated as the waters warm and open-water seasons extend , stimulating the bacteria and algae to thrive , coating everything with slime as they decompose organic matter ( note your E.coli water testing results will also fail more often ) . Water depths may also sometimes decline during severe drought , but what goes up must come down and increasingly we will experience more extreme water-level variability . <p> As for effective mitigation measures , we will need to pull out all the stops -- reduce our own fossil fuel use , plant more trees , protect wetlands , reduce nutrients ( soil , fertilizer , septic water ) , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ while actively giving support to those companies and governments prepared to tackle the source of the problem ( i.e. excessive fossil fuel use ) . In addition , we need to also prepare for failure , and to plan necessary emergency measures . <p> Eurasian watermilfoil : the plant is invading local lakes and rivers.Postmedia News files <p> Sudbury seems to have been spared many invasive species that have established themselves elsewhere , yet we do have Eurasian milfoil in several lakes and a plan to counter that with weevils had mixed results . What can we do to ensure existing invaders do n't multiply and new ones do n't show up ? <p> Eurasian milfoil ( Myriophyllum spicatum ) is like those relatives who come for Christmas with lots of luggage , but no return tickets -- they are not going home . Eurasian milfoil , as the name suggests , came to North America from Eurasia or maybe North Africa in about the 1940s ( probably as an aquarium plant or in the ballast water of ships ) . It hitch-hiked to Sudbury , presumably on the pontoons @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Lake in the late- ' 60s or early- ' 70s . The rest is history . <p> The Eurasian species of milfoil did encounter some close relatives here , the native northern milfoil ( M. sibiricum ) , but the invader easily displaced the locals and created dense beds of near-monocultures in many area lakes . The trick it used for this rapid spread was its ability to grow a whole plant from even a tiny broken fragment . Once established , Eurasian milfoil makes a nuisance of itself by clogging boat propellers , tangling fishing gear and spoiling the fun of jumping off the dock without having to worry about touching anything but water . When the beds get too dense or decompose under the ice , the reduced oxygen levels can also cause fish dieoffs . <p> Is there anything good about Eurasian milfoil ? Well , it does provide some fish habitat ( that is why you need to get permission from OMNRF before removing it around your dock ) , and like other aquatic plants such as cattails and reeds , it does protect the shoreline @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by too fast and too close to shore . <p> How can we manage it ? First do n't fragment it with your boat and do n't spread it to other lakes ( clean boats and trailers ) . After that , try to starve it to death by reducing the nutrients ( fertilizers , sewers , soil ) that flow to the lake from your property . Maybe like those pesky relatives , stop serving those big delicious meals , and perhaps they will decide to go home . <p> File Photo <p> is one of the oldest forms of life on Earth -- and the first , I believe , to perform photosynthesis -- but we understand it now as a problem . Why should we be so concerned about this plant proliferating in our lakes ? <p> Some of the details are a bit fuzzy , because it happened quite a few years ago , but what is clear is that life as we know it would not have occurred without the help of blue-green algae , more properly called cyanobacteria . These bacteria came into existence @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 1.5 billion years before Sudbury was hit by the meteorite , creating the Sudbury Basin ( 15 km deep , 200 km around ) and its ore body . The meteorite generated our future wealth , but long before that happened cyanobacteria were already doing amazing tricks -- they were beginning to enrich the atmosphere with oxygen , eventually pushing its concentration to today 's level of about 21 per cent . Even though life stayed in these pretty simple forms for another vast period of time , 1-2 billion years ago ( roughly speaking ) , other ancient bacteria-like critters happened to swallow some cyanobacteria whole . The relationship stuck and they grew together from then on . They were able to take advantage of the photosynthetic abilities ( powered by the sun just like solar panels are ) of the cyanobacteria within to start to supply their own energy needs . After that , it was off to the evolutionary races , with this symbiotic relationship later giving us higher forms of algae and plants . <p> Well , what 's wrong with our ancient distant relatives ? @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ or scums that float on the surface and look unpleasant and create a bad taste and smell in our drinking water . That is not the worst of it . Some of the many thousands of species of cyanobacteria produce a toxin that can irritate our eyes and skin and make us sick if we drink or swallow too many . Occasionally , dogs and other animals have actually died by consuming algal toxin . These are the reasons the health unit routinely samples for cyanobacteria and post warning signs when blooms occur . <p> What can we do ? Here again the biggest problem is excessive nutrients flowing into the lake . That is one of the reasons that the former environmental commissioner was so worried about the existence of so many locations in Ontario ( including Sudbury ) where sewers can overflow into storm drains and contaminate our lakes with both pathogens and nutrients ( yes , we also need to clean up pet waste near lakes ) . The other big problem is that cyanobacteria evolved to thrive in warmer conditions where rotting release of nutrients occurs @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ perfect storm that climate change poses for Sudbury 's urban lakes . <p> In an address to inaugurate the new addition of city council in early December , Mayor Brian Bigger emphasized the need to be " open for business " and spur economic growth , while saying little about the area 's natural attributes . A few years ago Canada 's Resourceful City was put forward as an alternative slogan for the City . How much does language and messaging matter ? <p> Nickel Capital of the World was a great slogan for its time , but My Sudbury did n't click with me . Resourceful City or Sudbury Solutions do suggest a place of advanced innovations and problem-solving , but how about Science City ( remember Dr. Art McDonald did walk out of the Creighton mine to pick up the Nobel Prize in Physics ) or City of Lakes ( 330 of these ) ? Would n't these also appeal to the " knowledge industry " or " quality of life " people ? <p> Getting rid of the moonscape reputation is the real challenge . The term @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ John Young and Charles Duke during their visit to Sudbury ( July 7 , 1971 ) when they we studying a meteor impact site ( Sudbury ) that was more accessible than those on the moon . They were n't trained geologists , but did succeed the next year to radioing back to Earth saying , " This looks like Sudbury rock . " <p> Unfortunately the moonscape tag stuck . Another blow came in 1972 when we commissioned Superstack as then the tallest smokestack in the world ( 381 metres ) , only to hear delegates at the first UN Global Conference on the Environment in Stockholm declare in the same year that countries should not pollute their neighbours in this way . Greenpeace activists did n't miss the irony and later protested in both Canada and Europe . However , our most regrettable statistic of once being the largest point source of SO2 in the world ( over two million tons/year ) in the ' 60s and ' 70s was the biggy . I should n't have been surprised when I attended my first international acid rain conference @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ participants using the term Sudbury as a unit of pollution . For example , " How many Sudburys does your country produce ? " <p> Changing such a bleak reputation is not easy , but a Nobel Prize at the SNOLAB is certainly a great help , as is the dazzling success of Science North , Ontario 's No. 1 tourist attraction in 2017 . However , I really think it was the incredible pollution reductions -- 99 per cent of sulphur emissions -- that has thrilled environmental scientists throughout the world and begun the real healing . ( Note : Sudbury 's Superstack is to be decommissioned in early 2020 ) . So too , when Sudbury representatives walked across the stage at the 1992 UN Earth Summit in Brazil to receive the Local Honours award for our massive regreening program ( 40th year this year ; 10 million trees planted ) . To add to this lustre , having a global scientist like Dr. Jane Goodall travel the world to show kids the " green leaf of hope from Sudbury " -- well , you could n't do @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ capitalized on Sudbury -- the city that Stats Canada designated in 2015 as " Happiest City in Canada " in 2015 with its affordable homes ( many are cottage-like on lakes ) and safe , vibrant multicultural community -- as a way of attracting more young people and families ( even my own kids ) to Sudbury ? I wish they would . <p> There has been a lot of groundbreaking research done in Sudbury , especially around acidification of lakes and their recovery from industrial impacts . What should the focus of scientific inquiry be now ? Is there research being currently carried out that excites you ? <p> Sudbury was at the centre of the acid rain debate in North America in the ' 70s and ' 80s , when we were the biggest source . Our Sudbury-born politician Jim Bradley was the environment minister and our local companies ( Inco and Falconbridge ) were showing a willingness to work with government if regulations were fair and even-handed . We also had the evidence , the data ( when science and facts mattered ) from a solid monitoring @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to occur with cleaner air . Industry also knew that they could improve energy and worker efficiency , convert much of the acid gases into marketable sulphuric acid , and make other changes to offset cleanup costs . This information proved critical to the negotiators who worked on revisions to the U.S. Clean Air Act in 1990 ( Brian Mulroney and W.H. Bush were the signatories ) . <p> Lots of great research has happened since these debates , and we have vastly grown our national and international collaborative network to continue to investigate all sorts of confounding factors that impact the recovery process of severely damaged lakes ( climate warming , calcium decline , " brownification , " forest effects , genetics , drought , trace metal interactions , microbiology , etc . ) . There are constant surprises -- that is how science develops , one failed explanation after another . A lot of the research effort has also expanded into the Far North to collect baseline data in advance of the Ring of Fire mining development , and the expected severe effects of climate change in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ subsistent food fishes , invasive species , fish community changes , etc . ) . <p> As for exciting current research at the Living with Lakes Centre by new researchers , I would first mention Dr. Nathan Basiliko who is leading a large nationally funded project designed to find better ways of sequestering carbon from the atmosphere while revegetating industrial-disturbed lands ( tailings , industrial barrens , etc . ) . Then there is the fascinating work that Dr. Nadia Mykytczuk is doing with her extensive network of colleagues using microbes to clean up toxic mine waste , while at the same time recovering valuable metals ( cobalt , nickel , copper , etc. ) to pay for the process . Both of these projects are the bases of exciting potential new clean-tech industries in Sudbury . <p> Road salt is one of Sudbury 's major environmental issues , John Gunn says.Supplled photo <p> Road salt entering Ramsey Lake was cited in the latest report from Ontario 's environmental commissioner as an example of a salinity trouble spot . What would it take to make Sudbury a salt-control exemplar ? @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ decades and we are now getting to the point where two potential effects of great concern may soon materialize : dense concentrations of green algae will occur and the property value of lakeside homes will decline . <p> The first threat ( greening of our lakes ) is because we depend on the free services of zooplankton , the tiniest animals in the lake , to graze down the suspended algae and prevent it from reaching concentrations where a thin pea-soup colour replaces the crystal-clear water we tend to prefer . Unfortunately , the hardworking zooplankton ( think tiny lawn mowers ) are particularly sensitive to road salt ( sodium chloride ) , which is now fast approaching toxic levels in many of our lakes for these helpful little creatures . As zooplankton die off , the algae may get denser and denser and reduce the clarity of the water , which then can reduce the property values of homes surrounding the lake . A detailed study in the State of Maine showed that declining water clarity can reduce the property value of a home by $200 or more for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ estimates for a lake like Ramsey , the loss would be more than $20 million . <p> What can we do ? Well , first we need to make sure that salt application is minimized and that all contractors are certified through the Smart About Salt training program . Right now the city usually adheres to many of these recommendations , but unfortunately many of the private contractors servicing the big-box stores and other heavy users of salt do not . These professional associations designed to reduce excessive salt use also offer better deals on liability insurance to limit public concerns about slipping or auto accidents . The other strategy is to look for alternative materials and approaches ( sand , specialized wood chip particles , heated sidewalks , etc . ) . Of course we should also stop feeding the algae ( fertilizers , sewage , eroded soil ) . <p> What about birds and other wildlife in Sudbury . What can you tell us about how the environmental cleanup has affected them ? Are they responding in the same way fish are ? <p> I need to start @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and I am often shocked that some people do n't actually like fish or at least do n't necessarily want fish to return to their lakes after the water quality has recovered . It is not that they actually hate fish -- it is just that they want their privacy instead , and do n't want to share " their lake " with anglers . That NIMBY sentiment is never true of loons . It does n't seem anyone hates loons , in fact some marvelous citizen scientists like Deiter and Marlise Schoenefeld are true loon lovers . The Schoenefelds have been meticulously monitoring loon families for decades in Sudbury lakes as part of the Canada Lakes Loon Survey . Through the years they have learned that when loon couples return from their winter holiday down south and choose a lake for nesting , they are then committed to feeding their new hatched young in that particular lake . However , if they have unfortunately chosen a lake that is acid- and metal-damaged , they are now basically stuck -- because they ca n't find enough food in such @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ravenous young ( in this case when the kids say they are starving , they really are ) . The sad ending is the chicks never develop enough to be able to fly south for the winter and have to be abandoned to die on the shore . <p> The good news is that in recent years Deiter and Marlise have documented that once the water quality improves ( result of pollution reduction ) to a point where those pesky fish can recolonize , the grocery basket is full again , the kids grow well , and the happy family spends their time waking up Sudbury folk with their haunting call all summer long before heading off together for their holiday . Lesson learned is , first , thank you Deiter and Marlise for the decades of great work . And of course we need fish . Fact : Fish provide over 25 per cent of the world 's protein needs and are one of the best sources of essential Omega 3 fatty acids.

@@60436960 <p> Highly adaptable Winnipeggers have a tendency to shrug off climate change . But all our flood-fighting knowledge will mean little if and when the sheer frequency of new climate-induced financial demands begin to hamper the way the city functions . <h> Rather than a catastrophe , new and numerous financial headaches threaten the city <p> Winnipeg looks idyllic on a sunny winter day . Politicians are starting to contemplate what it will cost when our climate becomes even more variable . ( Trevor Lyons/CBC ) <p> If you 're a 62-year-old office administrator with five grandchildren , a big mortgage and a mountain of credit-card debt , it 's a big deal to suddenly win $14.2 million in the lottery . <p> If you 're the City of Winnipeg , a windfall of that size means squat and diddly . <p> Based on financial figures from the end of November , the city is on track to post a $14.2-million surplus on all of its operations for 2018 . By the time the Dec. 31 accounting is done , the pool of black may be even larger . <p> While $14 million may sound like a lot of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a corporation the size of the City of Winnipeg . In 2018 , the city spent $1.08 billion on services that include everything from policing and fighting fires to clearing snow and filling potholes . <p> Failing to spend 1.3 per cent of that money does not mean the city is awash in money -- and anyone who makes that claim has n't been paying attention to Winnipeg or any other Canadian city . <p> Winnipeg remains a city with a serious financial problem , simply because the cost of delivering services tends to rise faster than the revenue that 's available to pay for those services . The severity of this problem is somewhat hidden if you only look at the city in any individual year . <p> That 's because unlike the province or the federal government , which are free to spend more money than they collect in any year , Winnipeg has no choice but to balance its budget . The city can incur debt , but it 's not allowed to post a deficit . <p> That 's why every calendar year in Winnipeg ends @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The bean counters at 510 Main St. run a very tight ship , at least when it comes to the accounting . <h> Cost-saving measures <p> This is not as simple as it might sound . In order to ensure spending matches income every year , every department in the city is expected to find ways to save cash . They include euphemistically named practices such vacancy management , which involves deliberately failing to fill empty positions in order to save cash , sometimes at the cost of operational efficiency and efficacy . <p> They may involve service cuts , such as the decision to no longer sweep leaf litter off city streets every fall . And up until recently , they involved draining money away from reserve funds set up to prevent financial ruin . <p> In 2017 , the city siphoned $5 million away from its financial stabilization reserve -- essentially , its rainy day fund -- in order to balance the budget without cutting $5 million worth of services or raising property taxes above the 2.33 per cent level promised by Mayor Brian Bowman . <p> This @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ where risk-management nerds start freaking out . In Canada , municipalities are advised to set aside no less than six per cent of their total budget in their financial stabilization reserve . <p> Right now , there 's about $65 million sitting in that fund . If city council observes the city 's own financial policies , that reserve fund will be topped up next month using the surplus from 2018 . <p> It 's tempting for politicians to avoid this practice . But Winnipeg needs its fiscal stabilization reserve fund now , more than ever . <p> That 's because the risk-management pendulum for Canadian cities has swung away from the happy-go-lucky days prior to the 2009 worldwide recession , when the answer to every municipal financial problem involved convincing Ottawa or the provinces to hand over more money . <p> Today , the doomsayers have the floor in any rational discussion about long-term financial risks . For starters , the federal government and most provinces are struggling too much with their own financial houses to give any serious consideration to cities . <p> Adding to this mundane scenario @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ economists expect this year or next . <h> Impacts of climate change <p> But the real buzzkill is climate change , which has already made its effect known on a number of Canadian cities . <p> Heat waves , like the ones that plagued Toronto and Montreal last summer , cost actual money in terms of emergency-service spending , energy costs and economic productivity . Forest fires and grass fires can threaten entire communities , droughts place restrictions on the use drinking and industrial water and even minor floods cause immensely expensive damage . <p> In Winnipeg , arguably one of the world 's most climate-adapted cities to begin with , we have a tendency to shrug off these risks . This city has proven adept at reducing per-capita water usage over the decades , digging out of periodic blizzards and protecting properties from both spring and summer floods . <p> The Red River Floodway is not just a drainage ditch . It 's a large-scale geo-engineering project designed specifically to deal with the eventuality of another major environmental disaster <p> But this can not make us smug . All @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and when the sheer frequency of new climate-induced financial demands begin to hamper the way the city functions . <p> To be clear , climate change likely wo n't wipe Winnipeg off the map the way boreal-forest fires threatened to burn away Fort McMurray in 2015 . The potential for a single , sudden , catastrophic disaster should not keep Brian Bowman or Brian Pallister up at night , assuming either of them gets a lot of sleep these days . <p> More realistically , climate change poses a threat to Winnipeg in terms of emerging financial costs and operational demands that will eventually place more demands on the city budget . <p> For an example of what a minor climate-related headache looks like , consider the emerald ash borer . In 2018 , Winnipeg suddenly had to allocate $1.3 million to start protecting trees against the invasive beetle , which threatens to decimate the city 's urban forest canopy . <p> While the presence of this particular organism can not be attributed to climate change , our slightly milder winters -- our January lows simply are n't as low @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of new invasive pests arriving . <p> A few million bucks wo n't break the bank . It may also not be enough to protect the urban forest canopy . <p> Future city budgets are bound to face a number of new insect-control , flood-mitigation , water-conservation and fire-protection demands , none of them meeting the disaster-scale threshold that could trigger financial aid from other levels of government . <p> Winnipeg is not equipped to deal with a series of new financial headaches , precisely because of the way its budgets are built every year . The city may be forced to deal with them through drastic measures that could go beyond the current menu of incremental service cuts or property-tax hikes . <p> Right now , the only tool the city has to weather the coming storm is the fiscal stabilization fund . How the city intends to deal with climate change , otherwise , is anyone 's guess . <p> " Those are precisely the questions we need to contemplate when putting together a multi-year budget , " city council finance chair Scott Gillingham ( St. James ) @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that we need to take a longer-term view of and consider the environmental impacts as we look at budgeting . " <p> Right now , Winnipeg only creates a single-year budget and that 's about to change . Consider that the next time someone grumbles about the city squirreling away a $14-million surplus for a rainier , stormier day . <h> About the Author <p> Bartley Kives <p> Reporter , CBC Manitoba <p> Reporter Bartley Kives joined CBC Manitoba in 2016 .
